effect: G1: a tax office that clears its backlog no longer collects up to a quarter more tax for good. The administration's collection ratio (PjA, outcomes.collectionRatio) multiplies every tax's collection efficiency (YBA inside cr); one of its terms rewards a fiscal-queue delay below the day-0 delay, ((delay0+.25)/(delay+.25))^.18, and once the backlog reaches zero that term was 1.25-1.43, so a few months on the fiscal priority (or a few more staff or offices) raised collection permanently: about +2% in rich countries and up to +25% in low-income ones (collection efficiency is capped at .99), and AI governments did it too through their backlog rule. Measured headless as the Philippines (tests/g1.headless.mjs, seed 12345): six months on the fiscal priority, then balanced, left the unmodified game's collection ratio at 1.25 and tax revenue at 18.7% of GDP against 16.2% at day 0; with the patch the ratio settles at 1.003 and revenue at 17.0%. The patch caps that delay term at 1.05 (at most +0.9% from a fast tax office); a delay longer than day 0 still lowers collection as before, and catching up a backlog still brings in its temporary extra (the processed/inflow term is unchanged). Revenue-administration reforms in practice add 1-3% of GDP over 5-10 years, not a quarter of revenue at once. G9: the administration spending line (gwA) also fell when collection rose, by 0.4 x the gain (up to 10% of the admin budget), a second reward for the same backlog trick (and for any ratio above 1, including a backlog catch-up or better integrity); it is now one-sided: worse collection still raises admin spending, better collection no longer cuts it. Day 0 unchanged (the delay term and the collection ratio are 1). No new state; saves load as before, but outcomes are recomputed each month, so a country already at the old 1.25 in a running save loses that extra collection the first month after the mod is switched on. (Minified names in this text are those of build 26335289.)
